content:
Dozens of pages from the President's Daily Brief were declassified on Friday—the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks—detailing what government officials knew about Osama bin Laden and al-Qaeda in the years leading up to the hijackings that killed nearly 3,000 people and reshaped American national security.

The documents show how intelligence analysts tracked bin Laden's movements and his support network, along with concerns about potential threats to U.S. targets, while also detailing officials' understanding of his networks in the United States and elsewhere—including how his operations were funded.

CIA Director John Ratcliffe called it an 'extraordinary act of transparency,' saying the trove represented the largest single declassification of President's Daily Briefs in CIA history—highly classified briefings prepared by the intelligence community for the government's top leaders.

The documents span from a February 1998 briefing prepared for then-President Clinton titled 'Terrorists Seek Weapons of Mass Destruction' that referenced bin Laden and other Islamic extremists, to a September 12, 2001, report in which a source said the attacks had been in the works for two years and that the U.S. Capitol was also a target.

An April 1998 document described the Taliban's reluctance to hand over bin Laden, who was seen as a 'guest' in Afghanistan, noting that they were 'grateful for the assistance he provided during the Soviet occupation' and therefore 'did not wish to antagonize him by monitoring or restricting his activities.'

A July 1998 briefing assessed that 'bin Laden is likely to place a high priority on conducting attacks inside the United States,' and noted that he was 'interested in using chemical and biological weapons to mount attacks.'

Two months later, a briefer wrote that bin Laden's 'preferred method of attack on the U.S. homeland is in Washington,' and that al-Qaeda 'may attempt to crash an aircraft loaded with explosives into a U.S. city.'

Potential hijackings were also discussed in December 1998, when a briefer described plotters who 'evaded security in a dry run at an unspecified New York airport,' and that 'some members of bin Laden's network have received hijack training.'

Other documents detailed bin Laden's pursuit of materials for a 'dirty bomb'—a conventional weapon mixed with radioactive material. Intelligence officials noted that by June 1999, his operatives had conducted experiments on explosives to 'increase their energy output.'

Roughly two years before the attacks, intelligence officials picked up on indications that bin Laden seemed to be concealing from the Taliban his true intent to launch unprovoked strikes against the United States. Briefings prepared for President Bush in early 2001 focused in part on bin Laden 'experimenting with crude methods to produce and deploy biological weapons.'

A report a month before the attacks stated that bin Laden was 'committed to carrying out terrorist attacks inside the United States,' and cited al-Qaeda's 1998 bombings of U.S. embassies as showing 'he will spend years preparing for attacks and will not be deterred by setbacks.'

At the time—in August 2001—officials wrote that 'suspicious activity in this country consistent with preparations for hijackings or other types of attacks has been observed, including recent surveillance of federal buildings in New York,' and added that the FBI was 'conducting approximately 70 full field investigations throughout the U.S. that it considers bin Laden-related.'

Many of the documents are redacted to conceal the names of sources and other identifying details. The files do not appear to yield any dramatic new findings about how the attacks were plotted or how U.S. officials understood events as they unfolded.

In the years after the attacks, a bipartisan commission pointed to a lack of intelligence sharing among agencies such as the CIA and FBI and made recommendations that led to the creation of new positions, including the Director of National Intelligence and the National Counterterrorism Center, which analyzes terrorism information from across the government at home and abroad.

The White House, asked for its response to the declassified documents, pointed to another set of records declassified Friday by the National Archives. Those included interview transcripts of national security officials from the Clinton and Bush administrations, the product of a commission that investigated the attacks from 2002 to 2004.
